text: Christopher Mark Luxon, born on 19 July 1970 in Christchurch to a Roman Catholic family of Irish, Scottish, and English descent, is a New Zealand politician and businessman who has served as the 42nd prime minister since 2023. A member of the National Party, he has been the Member of Parliament for Botany since 2020 and previously led the Opposition from 2021 to 2023. Before entering politics, he was the chief executive officer (CEO) of Air New Zealand from 2013 to 2019. Luxon grew up in Howick, East Auckland, studied commerce at the University of Canterbury from 1989 to 1992, earning a Master of Commerce (Business Administration), and worked part-time at McDonald's and as a porter at the Parkroyal Hotel during his school and university years. He joined Unilever in 1993, working in Wellington, Sydney, London, and Chicago, becoming president of Unilever Canada in 2008. He joined Air New Zealand as group general manager in May 2011 and became CEO in June 2012, leading the company to record profits through a booming tourism market, the elimination of underperforming regional routes, and job cuts. Air New Zealand was named Australia's most trusted brand multiple times during his tenure. In 2014, he joined the Virgin Australia board as a representative of Air New Zealand, which sold its 25.9% stake in 2016, leading to his departure from the board. He resigned from Air New Zealand in 2019 and was encouraged by former Prime Minister John Key to enter politics. He won the National Party candidacy for Botany in November 2019 after Jami-Lee Ross resigned, and was elected in 2020 with 52% of the vote. He was appointed spokesperson for local government, research, science, manufacturing, and land information, and associate spokesperson for transport in the Shadow Cabinet of Judith Collins. After Collins stepped down on 25 November, Luxon was named party leader on 30 November 2021, following the withdrawal of Bridges from the leadership race. In the 2023 general election, the National Party won 38.1% of the party vote and 48 seats, a plurality but not enough to govern, leading to negotiations with ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First that lasted six weeks and concluded on 24 November. A formal three-party coalition was formed, with separate agreements between National and each junior party, and Luxon was sworn in as prime minister on 27 November 2023 by Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro. Under his premiership, the Sixth National Government has implemented significant cuts to the civil service, including the elimination of 9,500 public sector jobs by May 2025 and the scaling down or cancellation of over 240 government programmes, amounting to approximately $6 billion in savings. The government introduced $14.7 billion in tax cuts, replaced the Three Waters reform programme with the Local Water Done Well policy, and reduced co-governance initiatives while discouraging the use of the Māori language in the public service. It also reintroduced the three-strikes sentencing law and launched a pilot military-style boot camp for youth offenders. The government contributed to the construction of the City Rail Link metro system in Central Auckland and agreed to support the Treaty Principles Bill to its first reading, though it stated it would not support the bill beyond that stage. Luxon defended the boot camp and the prison population growth, calling higher prisoner numbers a "good thing" and stating the cost would be "what the cost will be." The government repealed New Zealand's world-leading smoke-free legislation, returning around $1 billion in annual tax revenue, despite warnings from researchers that thousands of New Zealanders would die needlessly. Luxon also introduced a "traffic light" regime for welfare, requiring jobseekers to reapply every six months and introducing a community work sanction. In August 2024, he and Education Minister Erica Stanford announced a new mathematics curriculum to be introduced in early 2025 and confirmed the eventual scrapping of the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) over five years. In November 2024, he delivered a national apology to survivors of abuse in state and faith-based care and introduced legislation to ban strip searches on children and strengthen security checks for those working with children. In early 2025, he announced openness to abolishing regional councils as part of reforming the Resource Management Act 1991. In August 2024, he criticized so-called "nice to have projects" and called for local councils to focus on rubbish collection and water infrastructure, while also confirming Cabinet's agreement to revise the Local Government Act and scrap its four wellbeing provisions. In April 2024, he stripped Melissa Lee of her Media and Communications portfolio and Penny Simmonds of her Disability Issues portfolio during a cabinet reshuffle due to criticism over their handling of media and disability funding. On 5 May 2024, he and Simeon Brown announced that Auckland would avoid a 25.8 percent rates increase under the Local Water Done Well plan. In early August 2024, he visited Hawke's Bay to discuss post-flood and Cyclone Gabrielle relief, confirming that work on the Napier-Wairoa railway line would be paused to focus on State Highway 2, and announced a NZ$63 million contribution to remove sediment and debris. As of March 2024, his net worth was estimated between NZ$21 million and NZ$30 million, making him the second-wealthiest National Party leader after John Key, owning seven properties including a home in Remuera valued at NZ$7.68 million. In late 2024, he stated, "Let's be clear, I'm wealthy," in response to questions about his property sales. After becoming prime minister, he initially claimed a NZ$52,000 accommodation allowance, but later repaid all amounts received, stating the issue had become a distraction. He sold three properties in 2024, with Stuff estimating a potential profit of up to $769,500. As Leader of the Opposition, he used public funds to pay for Māori language lessons, stating it was relevant to his role, but once prime minister, the government considered discontinuing incentive payments for public servants to learn te reo. The government's economic policies, centered on tax cuts and reducing public spending, led to a protracted recession with per capita GDP falling 4.6% since September 2022, inflation peaking at 7.3%, unemployment rising from 3.7% in June 2023 to 5.2% by late 2025, and persistent GP shortages, with over 250,000 unregistered patients and productivity losses exceeding $1 billion annually. Emergency department wait times and staffing shortages have worsened, and despite efforts to recognize overseas qualifications and establish a third medical school, little progress has been made. Luxon has consistently defended the scale of job losses and public service cuts, and in August 2024, he warned young unemployed people that their "free ride" under Labour would end under National, stating the government would make sweeping cuts to the Ministry of Social Development in favor of privatised employment agencies. His coalition dynamics with deputy prime ministers Winston Peters and David Seymour have been controversial, as they have openly challenged his authority. In foreign policy, his government increased military spending and Five Eyes cooperation, reflecting a general pro-United States shift.

The Government introduced legislation to combat abuse in care, including banning strip searches on children and strengthening security checks for individuals working with children. In August 2022, Luxon warned young unemployed people that their "free ride" under Labour would end if National won the 2023 election, stating that under National, such benefits would end and that the Ministry of Social Development would face sweeping cuts in favour of privatised employment agencies, with no funding for failure. In August 2024, Luxon and Louise Upston announced a "traffic light" regime for welfare, introducing escalating consequences for beneficiaries who fail to meet job-seeking obligations; from early 2025, jobseeker beneficiaries must reapply for benefits every six months instead of annually, and a new community work sanction requiring beneficiaries to "build skills and confidence" was introduced. When interviewed on TVNZ and RNZ's Morning Report, Luxon could not answer questions about how much beneficiaries actually receive. In October 2025, Luxon and Upston confirmed that welfare eligibility for 18 and 19-year-olds would be tightened, with those whose parents earn over NZ$65,000 becoming ineligible for Jobseeker and other emergency benefits from November 2026; 18 and 19-year-olds with dependent children or who are estranged from their parents would remain eligible. Luxon stated: "We're here to help and support as much as we can, but you also have to take responsibility for that and actually just consigning you to a life of welfare for 18 years is unacceptable." Since becoming prime minister, Luxon has made overseas trips to Australia, the Pacific, Southeast Asia, Japan, and the United States, where he met Chinese leaders. According to The Economist and Foreign Policy, New Zealand's foreign policy under the National-led coalition has shifted away from China toward closer ties with its traditional Five Eyes partners—United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. During an interview with The Economist, Luxon said he was looking to "diversify New Zealand's diplomatic and trade relationships away from its reliance on China," a shift described as the country's biggest pivot since the 1986 ANZUS dispute over nuclear policy. Foreign Policy columnist Derek Grossman noted that Luxon and Foreign Minister Winston Peters were continuing a thaw in New Zealand–United States relations initiated under John Key in 2010 and continued by Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins, with examples including the Royal New Zealand Navy sailing through the Taiwan Strait and the government's expressed interest in AUKUS and NATO. In late August 2024, Luxon supported Taiwan's participation in the Pacific Islands Forum in response to Chinese efforts to exclude Taiwan from the 2025 event. In April 2025, the Government announced a $12 billion allocation for defence over four years, raising spending to 2% of GDP from 1%; this amount matches the Treasury's estimate needed to halve child poverty by 2028. The Child Poverty Action Group highlighted the auditor-general's criticism of the government for lacking a coherent plan to address rising child poverty, raising public concerns about defence spending versus social welfare. On 20 December 2023, Luxon made his first state visit to Sydney, meeting Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, reaffirming New Zealand's nuclear-free policy while expressing openness to joining the non-nuclear pillar of AUKUS and stating a commitment to "heavy lifting" in the Australia–New Zealand defence relationship. Between 9 and 10 August 2025, Luxon hosted Albanese in Queenstown for annual bilateral talks, discussing trade, defence, the Gaza war, and Australia's 501 deportation policy; local and civil society leaders including Mayor Glyn Lewers, MP Joseph Mooney, Ngai Tahu Tipene O'Regan, Edward Ellison, and Cliff Curtis attended. The leaders laid wreaths at a memorial to fallen ANZAC soldiers in Arrowtown on 10 August. Luxon has consistently opposed Australia's 501 deportation policy, calling it "regrettable" and "not right," especially when it results in people with minimal ties to New Zealand being deported; he expressed disappointment that Australia reversed its more lenient approach, which considered length of residence and family connections. He stated, "It's just not right that people who have no connection to New Zealand are deported to New Zealand." Following discussions with Albanese, Luxon said: "We respect the fact that Australia has its own policies around deportation," but hoped common sense would prevail. Luxon's leadership has been challenged by his coalition partners, David Seymour (ACT) and Winston Peters (NZ First), with concerns over his perceived lack of control. A 2024 poll found that 51% of respondents believed Luxon was the decision-maker. David Seymour has openly challenged Luxon's authority, particularly on the Treaty Principles Bill, and has publicly contradicted the prime minister, reinforcing perceptions of weak leadership; Seymour asserts Luxon cannot unilaterally sack ACT ministers. Winston Peters is seen as unpredictable and influential, having, for example, in March 2024, undercut Finance Minister Nicola Willis by claiming a $5.6 billion fiscal hole from her tax cuts. Luxon's background as a corporate executive has led to criticism of his communication style, including the use of business jargon such as referring to voters as "customers," and appearing out of touch. Janet Wilson, former chief press secretary for the National Party, said he memorises talking points and sounds like a "talking robot." Luxon has also been criticised for avoiding direct answers, notably during the Andrew Bayly resignation saga, when he sidestepped questions about whether he would have sacked Bayly, eventually conceding he would have "demoted" him and that "you can call it sacked," a performance widely described as evasive. His handling of the Treaty Principles Bill—supporting its introduction but pledging to vote against it later—has been seen as lacking conviction and clarity, with Luxon claiming that allowing a first reading was "worth it to form government." In April 2024, a 1News-Verian poll showed the coalition government behind the left bloc, with 51% of respondents believing Luxon was the decision-maker. A Talbot Mills poll suggested a Labour-led government would have a bare majority of 62 seats, while Roy Morgan found 54% of respondents believed New Zealand was heading in the wrong direction, with only 35% believing it was in the right direction. In June, a poll showed Luxon fell behind opposition leader Chris Hipkins in net favourability for the first time. Opinion polls indicate that Luxon's unpopularity has deepened over his first 18 months in office, with his net favourability lower than that of previous first-term prime ministers such as Helen Clark, John Key, and Jacinda Ardern. Max Rashbrooke, a senior research associate at Victoria University of Wellington, noted that a common criticism is Luxon's "inability to articulate what he stands for" or what he aims to achieve. In October 2025, The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll found that 27% of voters viewed Luxon positively, while 51% had an unfavourable view. Luxon is an evangelical Christian and a social conservative. In his maiden parliamentary speech, he described himself as centre-right and moderate; the government is described as conservative and right-wing, one of the most so since the 1990s. Luxon supports low taxes, cuts to the Ministry of Social Development, military-style boot-camps for young offenders, stringent anti-gang legislation, and opposes welfare dependency and co-governance with Māori. In November 2019, he said he was against abortion, euthanasia, and legalising recreational cannabis, though he supported medicinal cannabis; he previously supported a "no jab, no pay" policy for unvaccinated children, but after becoming leader of the National Party, he stated he did not support cutting benefits for parents who do not vaccinate children against COVID-19. He has also firmly opposed efforts to reform New Zealand's water system. His anti-abortion views drew media attention after his election as National leader; he confirmed his personal opposition to abortion but stated that National would not contest the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. After previously declining to answer whether he believed abortion was tantamount to murder, he said in an interview with Newshub that he is "a pro-life person," and when asked again, responded "that's what a pro-life position is." In response to the Gaza war, Luxon stated he was shocked and saddened by Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel, condemned Hamas's actions, and stated Israel had a right to defend itself. He committed New Zealand to active military support, saying "I want us to be in lockstep with our partners who have common interests and actually be right there with them at that time." In January 2024, he authorised the deployment of 6 NZDF personnel to support military action against Houthi forces in the Red Sea, stating it was about standing up for beliefs and demonstrating real capability. On 30 January 2024, Luxon announced New Zealand would suspend its annual NZ$1 million aid to UNRWA following allegations that some UNRWA workers participated in the October 7 attacks, following a Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade review of aid to UNRWA. On 29 February 2024, he designated Hamas in its entirety as a terrorist entity. As the Gaza war continued, Luxon's position evolved; on 2 December 2024, he confirmed New Zealand would comply with an International Criminal Court arrest warrant if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited New Zealand, stating: "We believe in the international rules-based system, we support the ICC, and we would be obligated to do so." In June 2025, he described sanctions on Israeli ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir as "entirely appropriate." On 9 August 2025, Luxon and Albanese called for a ceasefire in Gaza and opposed Israeli plans to occupy Gaza City. On 13 August 2025, Luxon made remarks in Parliament criticising Israel's conduct, describing it as "utterly, utterly appalling" and stating that "I think Netanyahu has gone way too far. I think he has lost the plot." In late November 2021, Luxon said conversion therapy was "abhorrent"; in early February 2022, he supported the LGBT+ community and announced National MPs would have a conscience vote on the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill, which passed its third and final reading on 15 February 2022, with Luxon voting in favour. Although he frequently criticised Labour's pandemic management, on 8 January 2022, he stated National strongly supported COVID-19 vaccination, describing it as the best protection for people and families. In response to US President Donald Trump's 2025 APEC announcement to resume nuclear testing, Luxon expressed disapproval and reiterated his commitment to New Zealand's nuclear-free policy. On 20 September 2024, Luxon said the coalition was open to holding a referendum to extend the parliamentary term from three to four years at the 2026 election. On 27 February 2025, the government introduced the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Bill to conduct a referendum. On 3 May 2023, Luxon acknowledged the historical sensitivity of the 1970s dawn raids, which disproportionately targeted Pasifika New Zealanders, but stated Immigration New Zealand needed to "reserve the option" to use police raids against individuals involved in serious criminal offending or posing a security risk. He also stated there were 14,000 overstayers in New Zealand, in response to media coverage of recent dawn raid tactics criticised by Deputy Prime Minister Carmel Sepuloni for re-traumatising the Pasifika community. On 11 December 2023, Luxon said New Zealand's 118,000 annual net migration rate was unsustainable and that infrastructure needed better management to support growth, following Australia's announcement of a new migration strategy. In late January 2023, Luxon stated National opposed co-governance in health, education, and critical infrastructure, though he supported "self-driven" Māori initiatives such as Whānau Ora, kohanga reo, and charter schools. On 25 January, he said the existence of Māori seats "doesn't make a lot of sense." During Waitangi Day on 6 February 2023, Luxon described the Treaty of Waitangi as a "challenging, imperfect but ultimately inspiring document" through which New Zealand sought to understand the intentions of those who signed it, acknowledging the Crown had not upheld its promises and expressing hope that the Treaty settlement process would be completed by 2030. During a Question Time on 20 August 2024, Luxon said he believed Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown by signing the Treaty, and when questioned by Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, reiterated that the Treaty was New Zealand's founding document and protected both Māori and Crown interests. On 19 December 2024, Luxon confirmed he would not attend events at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds on 4 February 2025, stating he intended to celebrate Waitangi Day across New Zealand with different iwi. National Waitangi Trust chairperson Pita Tipene expressed disappointment, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that Luxon's decision was not in line with the spirit of the Treaty.

During Waitangi Day on 6 February 2023, Luxon described the Treaty of Waitangi as a "challenging, imperfect but ultimately inspiring document through which New Zealand had sought to understand what was intended by those who signed it." While acknowledging that the New Zealand Crown had not upheld the Treaty's promises and obligations, he expressed hope that the Treaty settlement process would be completed by 2030. During a Question Time in Parliament on 20 August 2024, Luxon stated that he believed Māori ceded sovereignty to the New Zealand Crown by signing the Treaty of Waitangi, and reiterated that the Treaty was New Zealand's founding document, protecting both Māori and Crown interests. On 19 December 2024, Luxon confirmed he would not attend events at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds on 4 February 2025, stating his intention to celebrate Waitangi Day around New Zealand with different iwi; National Waitangi Trust chairperson Pita Tipene expressed disappointment with the decision, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Luxon was "running away from problems of his own creation." Luxon describes himself as a "soft republican" and believes New Zealand will "ultimately" become a republic, but that the change would not happen "in my Government and in my time." On 1 March 2025, Luxon said the school lunch programme was experiencing "teething issues" due to quality and delivery problems, adding that Associate Education Minister Seymour "will work his way through those issues... and I expect he will [find a solution]." On 4 March, during a press conference, he told parents dissatisfied with the programme to "make a marmite sandwich and put an apple in a bag," a remark that drew criticism from Hora Hora School principal Pat Newman, Child Poverty Action Group executive officer Sarita Divis, and East Otago High School principal Helen Newcombe, who argued that school lunches are needed to improve student health and educational outcomes and combat child poverty. In response, Luxon defended his remarks and reiterated the Government's commitment to resolving programme issues. In February 2024, Luxon stated that sex education should be age appropriate and that parents should be able to withdraw their children from such classes if they choose. In March 2023, when asked if anti-transgender activist Posie Parker should be allowed into New Zealand, Luxon affirmed people's right to free speech but said he "absolutely" supported the rights of New Zealand's transgender community. In mid-August, he said there is no need for laws specifying which toilets transgender people can use, and during a TVNZ debate with Prime Minister Chris Hipkins in September, he stated that transgender participation in sports should be left to sporting bodies. Luxon met his wife Amanda at a church youth group and they married on 8 January 1994 when he was 23; they have a son and daughter, and the couple share the same faith, saying "it quietly guides what they care about." In late July 2022, Luxon confirmed he was on a family holiday in Hawaii during the parliamentary recess when a Facebook video post on 21 July implied he was visiting Te Puke; he attributed the confusion to a delay in his social media team updating his whereabouts, which he called a mistake. Luxon had a Catholic upbringing but describes himself as a non-denominational Christian; after returning to New Zealand in 2011, he attended the Upper Room church in Auckland, but now does not go to a regular church, stating he doesn't even go to church every Sunday. In his maiden speech in Parliament, he said “My faith is personal to me. It is not in itself a political agenda.” Luxon has never drunk alcohol in his life, making that decision at about seven or eight years old, citing his grandfather's drinking problems as the reason. He enjoys DIY, listening to country music, waterskiing, and fishing; he is a supporter of the Crusaders rugby union team and Auckland FC in association football, attending Auckland FC's first ever A-League Men match in 2024, where he was pranked by a fan who flicked his nose while posing for a photo. Luxon has a long-standing friendship with former Prime Minister John Key, with whom he used to ask questions about the pros and cons of being a prime minister; in an interview with podcaster Dom Harvey, he said the friendship includes their wives, who spend considerable time together and try to catch up every weekend. He described the relationship as "really special" and said it is especially meaningful as a Prime Minister to have a former Prime Minister as a friend, though he emphasizes that when they talk, they are "mates first, and politics is second." In 2017, while Luxon was chief executive at Air New Zealand, John Key was appointed as an Air New Zealand director; both resigned from Air New Zealand in 2019. In 2015, Luxon was named the Deloitte Top 200 CEO of the Year for his leadership at Air New Zealand, and in 2019, he won a BLAKE Award for his sustainability initiatives at Air New Zealand.
